newsitem.title: USA: Mass. law means "unquantifiable" loss for tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Mass. law means "unquantifiable" loss for tobacco.

text.p: Tobacco companies, in court papers filed on Tuesday, claim they will suffer "unquantifiable" losses if a Massachusetts law demanding they reveal their cigarettes' ingredients is allowed to stand.

Philip Morris Co, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp and Lorillard Tobacco argue that the 1996 law will rob them of trade secrets and cause "losses of revenue, market share and good will...that are unquantifiable," according to the court papers.

Philip Morris, in a footnote to the papers filed with the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston, said its Marlboro brand "alone has been valued at over $44 billion, suprassing Coca-Cola as the most valuable brand in the world."
Marlboro accounts for 30 percent of the cigarettes sold in the United States, the papers said.
Philip Morris brands "account for nearly half of the U.S. domestic retail cigarette market," the papers said.

The court papers indicated that the effective date of the law, which requires the companies to submit a list of their brands' ingredients by weight to the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, appears to have been pushed back to November 1,1997 from July 1.

Reading like a badly done John Le Carre novel, the court papers detail the companies' extensive security procedures including: secret codes, locked boxes, stand alone computers and confidentiality agreements.

There is great discussion on "the great lengths to protect the confidentiality of ingredients and formulas" of each brand in the various affadavits submitted including limiting the formulas to only a few people "with a need to know."

Under the Massachusetts law, the companies would submit their brands' ingredients to the department of public health which would then review the list and submit it to the state attorney general's office, before posting the information on the Internet.
"A trade secret disclosed anywhere is destroyed everywhere," Henry Dinger, an attorney for Philip Morris, argued.
